name: Population below the poverty level
plain: Out of every 100 people the Census Bureau could classify, how many lived with income below the poverty level in the past 12 months. In Puerto Rico it was 40.5% in the 2020-2024 window.
definition: People whose income in the past 12 months was below the Census Bureau's poverty level (American Community Survey, ACS, table B17001, cell 2) divided by all people for whom the Bureau determines poverty status (B17001, cell 1), times 100. The Bureau does not determine poverty status for people in institutions such as prisons and nursing homes, in military group quarters or in college dormitories, or for unrelated children under 15. The poverty level depends on family size and the ages of its members, not on local prices.
unit: % of people for whom poverty status is determined
geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico; also 901 barrios and 981 census tracts

coverage.frequency: One estimate per five-year window, labeled by its last year (2010 = 2006-2010, 2024 = 2020-2024). A new window is added when the Census Bureau publishes it.

method: The observatory reads the table for every window: the per-sequence summary files for 2010-2020 and the table-based summary files for 2021-2024, for the 78 municipio rows and the Puerto Rico row. It divides cell 2 by cell 1. The margin of error of the share is computed by the observatory from the published margins of its parts, with the Census Bureau's formulas for sums (margins added in quadrature) and for a proportion whose numerator is part of the denominator. Puerto Rico's value comes from the island row of the same table.
source_detail: US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates, table B17001 (Poverty Status in the Past 12 Months by Sex by Age), cells 001 and 002; windows 2006-2010 to 2020-2024. Files, under https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/: for windows labeled 2021 to 2024, a table-based file such as 2024/table-based-SF/data/5YRData/acsdt5y2024-b17001.dat; for windows labeled 2010 to 2020, the per-sequence files in {year}/data/5_year_seq_by_state/PuertoRico/All_Geographies_Not_Tracts_Block_Groups/, where {year} is the last year of the window. Definitions follow the Census Bureau's ACS Subject Definitions (2024 edition: https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/tech_docs/subject_definitions/2024_ACSSubjectDefinitions.pdf; each earlier year has its own edition).
how_to_read: A value of 40 means that 40 of every 100 counted people lived below the poverty level. It counts people, not households, and it does not show how far below the line people are or for how long. The number after the plus-minus sign (±) is the margin of error. At 90% confidence, the true value probably lies within that distance of the estimate.
caveats: Neighboring windows share four of their five years. To judge change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2010-2014, 2015-2019 and 2020-2024 (labeled 2014, 2019 and 2024). See the entry on American Community Survey 5-year windows.
Income is measured over the 12 months before each household was surveyed, and interviews are spread across the five years of a window, so a window blends different years.
The poverty level is a national threshold. It is not adjusted for the cost of living in Puerto Rico.

Estimates for small municipalities are imprecise. The municipality profile warns for municipalities with fewer than 25,000 residents. The Full data dialog shows in italics any nonzero value whose margin of error is more than 30% of the estimate. Zero values and values with no published margin are not italicized, so an unmarked value is not proof of precision.

The Puerto Rico value is the Census Bureau's own island-level estimate, not an average of the 78 municipalities. The Housing page also prints the median of the 78 municipalities above each chart, which is a different number.

Also published for barrios and census tracts (acs_barrio.json and acs_tract.json), each value with its margin of error where the Census Bureau gives one. Below the municipality the figure is rough. In 2020-2024 the margin of error is above 30% of the estimate (the CSV by area marks such values as less reliable; no map or table draws areas below the municipality yet) for 53% of barrios and 35% of census tracts that have a value. See methods.small_area_estimates.
example: Puerto Rico, 2020-2024: 40.5% (± 0.4 points). Highest of the 78 municipalities in 2020-2024: Guánica, 63.7% (63.65 before rounding). Lowest: Guaynabo, 24.3%.

name: Median household income
plain: The middle household income in the area: half of households earn more, half earn less. Puerto Rico: $26,297 a year in the 2020-2024 window, in 2024 dollars.

Income means money income before taxes from wages, self-employment, interest, Social Security, retirement, public assistance and similar regular sources; it leaves out capital gains and non-cash benefits.

name: Maximum affordable 30-year loan
plain: The largest 30-year home loan a household with the area's median income could carry. The method assumes the household spends 30% of its income on housing. About 78% of that budget goes to the loan payment, at a fixed 5% interest rate. Puerto Rico: $95,921 in the 2020-2024 window. It is a yardstick, not a lender's limit.
definition: A calculation on median household income (American Community Survey, ACS, table B19013). Monthly housing budget = income × 0.30 / 12. Loan payment = budget × 430/549 (about 78.3%, the share of the housing budget that the study's Table 6 puts on principal and interest). Maximum loan = payment × (1 - (1 + r)^-360) / r, with r = 0.05 / 12, rounded to whole dollars.
unit: US dollars (loan amount), in the dollars of the last year of each five-year window

coverage.frequency: One estimate per five-year window, labeled by its last year (2010 = 2006-2010, 2024 = 2020-2024). A new window is added when the Census Bureau publishes it.

method: The observatory applies the formula in the definition to the median household income of each municipality and of Puerto Rico in each window. The 30%, the 430/549 and the rate are fixed. The study prints no interest rate; the 5% is inferred from its Puerto Rico row (see the caveats). It is held fixed in every window, so windows differ only through incomes. No margin of error is calculated.
source_detail: Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR) calculation (State of Housing 2023, Table 6 method) on US Census Bureau ACS 5-year table B19013, cell 001; windows 2006-2010 to 2020-2024. The study PDF at the link above numbers this table 8; the Housing page and this dictionary call it Table 6. Files, under https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/: for windows labeled 2021 to 2024, a table-based file such as 2024/table-based-SF/data/5YRData/acsdt5y2024-b19013.dat; for windows labeled 2010 to 2020, the per-sequence files in {year}/data/5_year_seq_by_state/PuertoRico/All_Geographies_Not_Tracts_Block_Groups/, where {year} is the last year of the window. Definitions follow the Census Bureau's ACS Subject Definitions (2024 edition: https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/tech_docs/subject_definitions/2024_ACSSubjectDefinitions.pdf; each earlier year has its own edition).
how_to_read: Read it as: the loan size that this method says the typical household can support. If the typical home costs more than that, the typical household is priced out under the method. It is a way to compare places and years, not a prediction of what a bank would lend. The ratio of home value to this loan is the affordability ratio.
caveats: The method makes five assumptions: 30% of income goes to housing; about 78% of that goes to principal and interest (the rest to taxes, insurance and other costs); a 30-year loan; a 5% interest rate in every window; and the median household income is the buyer's income. Change any one and the answer changes. It does not assess whether any household can buy a home or qualify for a loan, and it is not financial advice.

The study prints no interest rate. The 5% rate is inferred from the study's Puerto Rico row: $21,967 of income and an $80,181 maximum loan imply 4.994%. At exactly 5% the observatory's figures are $19 to $65 below the printed maximums.
Real mortgage rates changed over the period (the Housing page notes they ranged from under 4% to over 7%), so the figure is not what a lender would have offered in any one year.
It leaves out down payments, closing costs, other debts, credit history and lender rules. It also ignores that the median household is not necessarily a buyer.
It carries the sampling error of median household income, but no margin is shown for it.

Dollars are those of the last year of each five-year window (2024 dollars for 2020-2024), as the Census Bureau states them. Amounts from different windows are not in the same dollars. To compare across windows, use the Analysis tab's Inflation-adjusted option, which restates dollars with the US Consumer Price Index (see the entry on inflation adjustment).

Neighboring windows share four of their five years. To judge change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2010-2014, 2015-2019 and 2020-2024 (labeled 2014, 2019 and 2024). See the entry on American Community Survey 5-year windows.
example: Puerto Rico, 2020-2024: median household income $26,297 gives a maximum loan of $95,921. Highest of the 78 municipalities in 2020-2024: Guaynabo, $170,456. Lowest: Las Marías, $59,507.

plain: How many times the typical home's value is larger than the largest loan the typical household could carry. Above 1.0, the typical home is out of reach for the typical household under the study's method. Puerto Rico: 1.37 in the 2020-2024 window.

how_to_read: A ratio of 1.37 means the typical home is worth 37% more than the largest loan the typical household could carry. Values at or below 1.0 mean it is within reach under the method. The Housing page colors a municipality 'out of reach' when the ratio is above 1.00 and 'within reach' otherwise.
caveats: Both medians describe different groups: home value is for owner-occupied homes and owners' own estimates, while income is for all households, renters included. The ratio is a yardstick, not a measure of what buyers face for homes on the market. It does not assess whether any household can buy a home or qualify for a loan, and it is not financial advice.
It carries all the assumptions of the maximum affordable loan: 30% of income, 78% to principal and interest, a 30-year loan and a fixed 5% rate.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, the ratio is above 1.0 in all 78 municipalities in every window from 2010 to 2023. In 2020-2024 it is above 1.0 in 76 of 78; Culebra (0.97) and Guayanilla (1.00) are at or below 1.0.

Near 1.0 the label is not reliable: no margin is calculated, and the ratio is rounded to two decimals before the page labels it. Guayanilla in 2020-2024 (ratio 1.00 after rounding; $87,400 value against an $87,232 maximum loan) is labeled 'within reach' although its value is slightly above the loan. In the 2026-10 snapshot, four municipalities lie between 0.95 and 1.05 in 2020-2024 (Culebra 0.97, Guayanilla 1.00, Patillas 1.01, Gurabo 1.03). Treat ratios in that range as at the line.
Value and income come from the same window, so they are in the same dollars. Small municipalities have noisy medians, and the ratio multiplies that noise; no margin is shown.

Neighboring windows share four of their five years. To judge change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2010-2014, 2015-2019 and 2020-2024 (labeled 2014, 2019 and 2024). See the entry on American Community Survey 5-year windows.
example: Puerto Rico, 2020-2024: median home value $131,500 divided by a maximum loan of $95,921 gives 1.37. Highest of the 78 municipalities in 2020-2024: Aguadilla, 1.92. Lowest: Culebra, 0.97.

name: Households approved for FEMA housing assistance
plain: The number of households FEMA (the Federal Emergency Management Agency) approved for help after disasters declared in a given year, by municipality. It counts approvals, not damage. It does not show how many homes were hurt or how much help people needed.
definition: Sum, over the disasters declared in a calendar year, of the number of applicants approved for FEMA's Individuals and Households Program (IHP) in the municipality. It adds the OpenFEMA Housing Assistance data for owners and for renters (field approvedForFemaAssistance). The year is the year of the disaster declaration.
unit: households (applicants approved for FEMA assistance), by year of disaster declaration

coverage.frequency: One value per year that had a disaster declaration with housing assistance records. In the 2026-10 snapshot these years are 2003, 2004, 2008, 2011, 2017, 2020 and 2022. The data are not live: they are downloaded from OpenFEMA when the observatory's data are refreshed and kept until the next refresh. The values in the 2026-10 snapshot come from the download of 2026-10-02 and can change if FEMA revises its records.

method: The observatory reads the OpenFEMA API (v2) entities HousingAssistanceOwners and HousingAssistanceRenters for Puerto Rico, matches each county (the municipality) to the 78 municipalities, takes the year of each disaster from DisasterDeclarationsSummaries (declarationDate), and adds approvedForFemaAssistance for owners and renters and across the disasters of the year. Puerto Rico's value is the sum of the 78 municipalities (the one 'statewide' record holds zero). No margin of error.
source_detail: FEMA OpenFEMA, Housing Assistance Program Data, Owners and Renters (v2), field approvedForFemaAssistance; disaster years from OpenFEMA Disaster Declarations Summaries. Years with data in the 2026-10 snapshot: 2003 (severe storms, flooding, mudslides and landslides; disaster no. 1501), 2004 (Tropical Storm Jeanne; 1552), 2008 (severe storms and flooding; 1798), 2011 (Hurricane Irene, 4017, and Tropical Storm Maria, 4040), 2017 (Hurricane Irma, 4336, and Hurricane Maria, 4339), 2020 (the COVID-19 pandemic declaration, 4493; earthquakes, 4473; Hurricane Isaias, 4560; a severe storm and flooding, 4571) and 2022 (Hurricane Fiona, 4671, and a severe storm, flooding and landslides, 4649). API endpoints: https://www.fema.gov/api/open/v2/HousingAssistanceOwners and https://www.fema.gov/api/open/v2/HousingAssistanceRenters (state eq 'PR'). Dataset pages: https://www.fema.gov/openfema-data-page/housing-assistance-program-data-owners-v2 and https://www.fema.gov/openfema-data-page/housing-assistance-program-data-renters-v2. Disaster years: https://www.fema.gov/api/open/v2/DisasterDeclarationsSummaries.
how_to_read: Read each value as 'households approved for help after disasters declared in that year'. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island totals are 475,798 households in 2017 (Irma and Maria) and 741,313 in 2022 (Hurricane Fiona and a severe storm with flooding and landslides). This is a count, so larger municipalities show larger numbers (San Juan is highest in both years). The number of approvals and the dollars do not move together: 2022 has more approvals than 2017 but about half the dollars (see the approved amount). The data do not explain this difference.
caveats: It measures aid approved, not damage, need or the number of homes affected. Who applies and is approved depends on FEMA rules and on people's access to the process.

OpenFEMA describes the counted field as the number of FEMA applicants approved for assistance. The observatory calls them households; the data the observatory keeps hold no household identifier, so they cannot show whether two applicants share a home.

Counts are added across the disasters declared in the year. A household approved under two disasters in the same year (for example Irma and Maria in 2017) is counted once for each disaster under which it was approved.

The Analysis tab's 'Per 1,000 residents' option divides households by residents, so it is not a share of households. Do not divide by the number of households to get a share: for scale, in the 2026-10 snapshot the 2022 approvals equal about 61% of the island's 1,219,658 households in the 2018-2022 American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates (95% in Orocovis), and a household approved under both declarations of a year is counted twice.

The year is the year of the disaster declaration, not the year of the damage or of the payment. In the 2026-10 snapshot, on the Housing page a year without a declaration shows the most recent earlier year: 2010 shows the 2008 values, 2012 to 2016 show 2011, 2018 and 2019 show 2017, 2021 shows 2020 and 2023 to 2025 show 2022. The data file has no value for those years.
Values for 2017 and 2020 combine several declarations and cannot be split by disaster in the observatory. A declaration is listed here only because OpenFEMA holds housing assistance records under it.

A municipality with no value in a declaration year has no approved-assistance record for it in the data; that is not proof that the municipality was untouched. The earliest year in the data is 2003, and OpenFEMA's dataset page says the housing assistance data cover disasters declared from November 2002 onward, so a missing earlier year does not mean there was no aid. In the 2026-10 snapshot, only 21 municipalities have values for 2003 and 2008, 34 for 2011 and 60 for 2004; 2017 and 2022 have all 78, and 2020 has 77.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, the municipality profile shows the sum of all years in the data (2003 to 2022) with the note 'all disasters'; households approved in more than one disaster are counted more than once.

Individual Assistance for households only. Other FEMA money (Public Assistance for governments, hazard mitigation), insurance payouts, Small Business Administration loans and disaster-recovery grants from the US Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) are not included.

On its dataset page (https://www.fema.gov/openfema-data-page/housing-assistance-program-data-owners-v2, as of 2026-10-04), OpenFEMA states that the data are self-reported and subject to human error, that the county is inferred by the system and may be overridden by the applicant, and that the financial information comes from FEMA's internal National Emergency Management Information System (NEMIS), not its official financial systems, may differ slightly from usaspending.gov and is not intended for official federal financial reporting.

OpenFEMA data are US government data under the OpenFEMA terms. The terms ask users to name the data set (Housing Assistance Program Data, Owners and Renters, v2) and the date retrieved (2026-10-02) and to state that the product is not endorsed by FEMA; the credit line under the Cite button includes that statement. Check the OpenFEMA terms before reuse.

API endpoints: https://www.fema.gov/api/open/v2/HousingAssistanceOwners and https://www.fema.gov/api/open/v2/HousingAssistanceRenters (state eq 'PR'). Dataset pages: https://www.fema.gov/openfema-data-page/housing-assistance-program-data-owners-v2 and https://www.fema.gov/openfema-data-page/housing-assistance-program-data-renters-v2. Disaster years: https://www.fema.gov/api/open/v2/DisasterDeclarationsSummaries.
how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island totals are $1,348,391,207 in 2017 (Irma and Maria) and $650,531,031 in 2022 (Hurricane Fiona and a severe storm with flooding and landslides). It is a total, so large municipalities show large amounts; divide by residents or households to compare places. On the Analysis tab, a shaded layer starts as dollars per resident (see 'Dollars per resident').
caveats: It measures aid approved under one FEMA program, not damage, need or money received. OpenFEMA labels the field as the total amount approved.

The amounts are totals approved to FEMA applicants (owners and renters). The observatory calls them households; the data the observatory keeps hold no household identifier, so two applicants who share a home cannot be told apart.

Amounts are as OpenFEMA records them and are not adjusted for inflation. The data hold no approval date and no price year, so an amount cannot be tied to a price year: values are totals as of the download, grouped by the year of the disaster declaration. The Analysis tab can restate them with the national Consumer Price Index (CPI-U), treating each amount as dollars of the declaration year; this is an approximation, because a national index may not match price changes in Puerto Rico.

The year is the year of the disaster declaration, not the year of the damage or of the payment. In the 2026-10 snapshot, on the Housing page a year without a declaration shows the most recent earlier year: 2010 shows the 2008 values, 2012 to 2016 show 2011, 2018 and 2019 show 2017, 2021 shows 2020 and 2023 to 2025 show 2022. The data file has no value for those years.
Values for 2017 and 2020 combine several declarations and cannot be split by disaster in the observatory. A declaration is listed here only because OpenFEMA holds housing assistance records under it.

A municipality with no value in a declaration year has no approved-assistance record for it in the data; that is not proof that the municipality was untouched. The earliest year in the data is 2003, and OpenFEMA's dataset page says the housing assistance data cover disasters declared from November 2002 onward, so a missing earlier year does not mean there was no aid. In the 2026-10 snapshot, only 21 municipalities have values for 2003 and 2008, 34 for 2011 and 60 for 2004; 2017 and 2022 have all 78, and 2020 has 77.

Individual Assistance for households only. Other FEMA money (Public Assistance for governments, hazard mitigation), insurance payouts, Small Business Administration loans and disaster-recovery grants from the US Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) are not included.

Some of this money may also be counted in the federal award series ('Federal awards, all types'). The observatory has not reconciled the two, and they use different time bases (the year of the disaster declaration here, the date of each award transaction there). Do not add them.

On its dataset page (https://www.fema.gov/openfema-data-page/housing-assistance-program-data-owners-v2, as of 2026-10-04), OpenFEMA states that the data are self-reported and subject to human error, that the county is inferred by the system and may be overridden by the applicant, and that the financial information comes from FEMA's internal National Emergency Management Information System (NEMIS), not its official financial systems, may differ slightly from usaspending.gov and is not intended for official federal financial reporting.

OpenFEMA data are US government data under the OpenFEMA terms. The terms ask users to name the data set (Housing Assistance Program Data, Owners and Renters, v2) and the date retrieved (2026-10-02) and to state that the product is not endorsed by FEMA; the credit line under the Cite button includes that statement. Check the OpenFEMA terms before reuse.

name: The State of Housing in Puerto Rico (2023): figures and tables on the Housing page
plain: The Housing page reproduces tables and headline figures from the Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR) 2023 study 'The State of Housing in Puerto Rico'. definition: The file housing.json has eight top-level fields: lihtc (Table 10, six projects that use the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit, LIHTC); headline (four figures); citation (the study reference); links (four web addresses); and grapi, smocapi, renters_burdened_pct and owners_burdened_pct (two island-wide cost-burden distributions and their sums, recomputed from the Census Bureau's 2020-2024 data with the method of Tables 3 and 4). method: The observatory builds the file with each snapshot: the published figures are typed as printed; the distributions are summed from the American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year tables for the 78 municipalities. name: Table 6: Home ownership affordability by age of householder
plain: The largest 30-year home loan a Puerto Rico household could carry, by age of the householder (the person in whose name the home is owned or rented), if it spends 30% of its income on housing. For all households the study found a maximum of $80,181 on a median income of $21,967. The page repeats the arithmetic for every five-year window from 2010 to 2024.
definition: Table 6 of the study has five rows (all households and four age groups of the householder: 15-24, 25-44, 45-64, 65 and over) and five columns: the age range, the median income of the age group (dollars per year), 30% of income for housing (dollars per month), the part of that paid as principal and interest (dollars per month), and the maximum 30-year mortgage (dollars). The page shows the published table, then the same arithmetic on Census Bureau incomes for the selected window.
unit: US dollars (income per year; payments per month; loan amount)

coverage.frequency: The published table is fixed. The live version has one table per five-year window, labeled by its last year.

method: Published: typed into site/js/housing.js as printed. Live: the observatory reads American Community Survey (ACS) table B19049 (median household income by age of householder), cells 1 to 5 for Puerto Rico, in housing_series.json under tables.t6_income_by_age. The page then computes in the browser: housing budget = income × 0.30 / 12; principal and interest = budget × 430/549; maximum mortgage = principal and interest × (1 - (1 + r)^-360) / r with r = 0.05 / 12. The same method gives max_affordable_loan for each municipality.
source_detail: Foundation for Puerto Rico (2023). The State of Housing in Puerto Rico: An Analysis of the Factors That Impact Housing and Rent Prices in Puerto Rico and Proposed Strategies to Increase Housing Affordability. Advancing Equitable Neighborhood Development grant, funded in part by NALCAB (National Association for Latino Community Asset Builders). Table 6 (US Census 2021). Live: US Census Bureau, ACS 5-year table B19049 (Median Household Income in the Past 12 Months by Age of Householder), cells 001-005. In the study PDF this table is numbered Table 8. Study PDF: https://foundationforpuertorico.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/state_of_housing.pdf
how_to_read: Read across a row: income, then the monthly budget, then the share for the loan, then the loan. The page notes that the study puts the median value of housing units at $111,800 (study, p. 22) and most homes available at asking prices of $90,000 and up.
caveats: The five published median incomes equal the observatory's values for the 2017-2021 window (labeled 2021) in table B19049, so the study's 'US Census 2021' matches the observatory's 2017-2021 window.
The page labels the first row 'Puerto Rico avg.'; the value is the median household income of all households (table B19049, cell 1), not an average.

The study prints no interest rate. The 5% rate is inferred from the study's Puerto Rico row: $21,967 of income and an $80,181 maximum loan imply 4.994%. At exactly 5% the observatory's figures are $19 to $65 below the five printed maximums.
The 78% share for principal and interest ($430 of $549) is the study's own proportion; the rest of the budget is left for taxes, insurance and other costs.
Dollars are those of the last year of each five-year window and are not adjusted across windows.
A maximum loan is a yardstick, not a lender's limit: it ignores down payments, other debts and lending rules.
The observatory does not store margins of error for the live income figures. Small groups, such as householders aged 15-24 ($7,826 in 2017-2021, $13,337 in 2020-2024), can move a lot between windows.

name: Table 10: Low-Income Housing Tax Credit projects funded with CDBG-DR

plain: A card for any one of the 78 municipalities, based on the study's Table 11 case study of Ceiba. It lists the study's variables and the housing indicators for the selected year, with each value's rank among the 78 and a small trend line.

The FEMA row adds all disasters since 2003, so a household approved under more than one disaster is counted more than once.

name: Headline figures from the study: housing units, vacancy, abandonment and the yearly housing deficit
plain: The study gives four round numbers. In 2020, Puerto Rico had about 1.6 million housing units and 370,000 vacant homes. The 370,000 is not the 2020 census-day count in the observatory, which is 257,625. The study estimates 300,000 units are dilapidated or abandoned. It cites a government estimate of 20,000 new homes needed each year.
definition: Four headline figures shown at the top of the Housing page and quoted in its text: housing units in 2020 (1,600,000), vacant homes in 2020 (370,000), an estimate of dilapidated or abandoned units (300,000) and the annual new-housing deficit (20,000, a government estimate). The same row on the page also shows the study's 2020 resident count of 3,285,694 (see Table 2). The Census Bureau's April 2020 count is 3,285,874, which is 180 higher (see 'Resident population').
unit: housing units (count)

coverage.frequency: Fixed as published; not updated.

method: Stored in housing.json under headline as printed, rounded. The page labels the first two 'Census 2020, study p.14', the third 'study p.14' and the fourth 'study, regulation brief 2024'.
source_detail: Foundation for Puerto Rico (2023). The State of Housing in Puerto Rico: An Analysis of the Factors That Impact Housing and Rent Prices in Puerto Rico and Proposed Strategies to Increase Housing Affordability. Advancing Equitable Neighborhood Development grant, funded in part by NALCAB (National Association for Latino Community Asset Builders). p.14 and the 'regulation brief 2024' that the page cites for the 20,000 figure (the observatory does not hold the brief). Study PDF: https://foundationforpuertorico.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/state_of_housing.pdf
how_to_read: Use them as orders of magnitude. For exact counts use the live series: census-day housing units and vacant units for 2010 and 2020, and American Community Survey (ACS) housing units and vacant units for every window.
caveats: The observatory's own 2020 census-day count is 1,598,159 housing units (rounds to 1.6 million) but 257,625 vacant units, so the study's 370,000 vacant homes does not match it. The 370,000 is close to the American Community Survey estimates of vacant units: 368,182 for the 2015-2019 window and 354,227 for 2016-2020. The page labels the figure 'Census 2020, study p.14'. Treat it as the study's figure, not as the 2020 census count.
The 300,000 abandoned or dilapidated units is an estimate, not a count. The nearest public proxy in the observatory is 'other vacant' units (219,965 in the 2016-2020 window).
The 20,000 homes a year is a government estimate cited by the study. The observatory does not hold the source, and the page labels it "study, regulation brief 2024". Cite it as the study's figure.
